Fall 2026

01

What is A.I.?

Broderick Shoemaker

Monday, August 31

01The question

Seriously — what is it?

The term gets thrown around all the time but it doesn't seem clear there's an agreed upon definition for it. 

Wikipedia: 
Artificial intelligence (AI) is the capability of computational systems to perform tasks typically associated with human intelligence, such as learning, reasoning, problem-solving, perception, and decision-making. It is a field of research in engineering, mathematics, and computer science that develops and studies methods and software that enable machines to perceive their environment and use learning and intelligence to take actions that maximise their chances of achieving defined goals.[1]


02some ideas from The people who built it

Turing · 1950
“Can machines think?” is “too meaningless to deserve discussion,” so he trades it for a question that can be settled: a questioner types to a hidden person and a hidden machine and has to say which is which. If no one can tell them apart, he argues, the first question stops mattering. What the test measures is behaviour — it says nothing about thinking.
McCarthy · 1955
“Every aspect of learning or any other feature of intelligence can in principle be so precisely described that a machine can be made to simulate it.” He names the field in a grant application.
von Neumann · 1958
He didn't define it but saw a danger: technology accelerating toward “some essential singularity in the history of the race beyond which human affairs, as we know them, could not continue.” Secondhand, from Ulam, the year after he died.
Minsky · 1968
“Making machines do things that would require intelligence if done by men.” The definition points back at us — the machine never has to have any of its own.

03Some more quotations

Dreyfus · 1965
The attempt to reduce intelligence to symbols manipulated by rules. He argued that is the whole programme, and that it cannot work: human skill is held in a body and a situation, not in a rulebook.
Searle · 1980
Symbol shuffling, not understanding. His test case: a man locked in a room is passed notes in Chinese and looks each character up in a rulebook that tells him which characters to write back. His replies read as fluent Chinese. He has learned the shapes and not one word of the language — and Searle says a computer is doing exactly that, no matter how good the replies get.
Russell & Norvig · 1995
Something that senses its surroundings and acts to get the best outcome it can. The textbook drops thinking altogether. A thermostat qualifies. So does ChatGPT.
Tesler
“Intelligence is whatever machines haven’t done yet.” Chess was A.I. until a computer won. Now it is a chess program.
Amodei · 2024
“A country of geniuses in a datacenter.” Anthropic’s chief executive, whose company is valued on that sentence turning out to be true.


ELIZA · a transcript, or the elizabot window

04Weizenbaum · 1976

“…extremely short exposures to a relatively simple computer program could induce powerful delusional thinking in quite normal people.”

He wrote ELIZA ten years earlier to show how little was going on inside it. It reflects your sentence back as a question — that is the whole program — and people confided in it anyway.

Computer Power and Human Reason, 1976.

Chat with it: masswerk.at/elizabot

05What the thing in this class actually is

“A large language model is a sophisticated mathematical function that predicts what word comes next for any piece of text.”

3Blue1Brown · LLMs explained briefly

Not a mind, not a database. A function: text in, a probability spread over every possible next word out, sampled once, then run again on its own output. That loop is the entire product.

Where do the numbers in that function come from? They were fitted to an enormous pile of human writing. That is why predicting one word at a time produces grammar, facts and style at all — and why it also reproduces whatever was wrong in the pile.
